answers.answer: Caching could replace repeated 80 ms guide construction with a 2 ms cache lookup for popular station-language pairs, which change infrequently. Use a key such as station:42:guide:es, including both station ID and language. On a hit the API returns the cached guide. On a miss the API reads/builds the guide from the database, stores the resulting copy in the cache, and returns it. The cache does not fetch it itself. A miss still incurs the database work plus the cache lookup and cache write; copies also use memory. The database remains authoritative.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours: A stores its previously fetched old value after B has committed and deleted the key. Deletion removed the copy at that moment but did not stop a paused reader from putting an old value back. The team cannot claim every read after B finishes sees the new hours. For this endpoint, read the authoritative database for each request instead of serving this cached copy; a subsequent database read sees the committed hours under the stated prerequisite.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

answers.answer: In case A, 12:03 can return the original cached forecast, even though it is stale after the 12:02 source change. At 12:11 the original entry has expired, so the API must fetch the source and fill a new copy. In case B, the 12:04 memory removal leaves no entry for 12:05, so that request must fetch the source even though ten minutes have not elapsed. The TTL limits how long that entry may remain before expiration; it does not refresh the source automatically or promise the forecast remains current during those ten minutes, and it does not bound the age of the data originally fetched. Memory removal is eviction to free space, a separate reason for disappearance that can happen before expiration.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.
A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.

answers.answer: A single shared cache entry is the simpler fit for making one deletion remove the map used by all four instances. Today each lookup happens inside the receiving API process; deleting the writer instance's copy leaves the other three copies available, so requests routed to those instances can still return the old map. With a shared cache each instance makes a network lookup to a separate service, and deleting the single entry makes subsequent lookups miss for every instance under the stated no-concurrent-fills assumption. This adds the accepted network cost and service operation. Losing one local cache affects only that instance's copy; the other instances retain theirs. An unreachable shared cache prevents all four instances using it from accessing its entries. Sharing does not itself keep the database and cache synchronized.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.
Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.

answers.answer: Single-key expiration makes many simultaneous requests miss and repeat the same schedule database read, potentially overwhelming the 500-reads-per-second capacity. Coalesce requests for that key: one request starts the database lookup and concurrent requests share its pending result, so the burst produces one lookup instead of one per request, then the API can cache the result. During the separate outage, sending all 10,000 requests per second to the database would far exceed capacity. Cap database fallback at no more than its safe 500 schedule reads per second and return temporary errors for excess requests. If a last known schedule is available outside the unreachable cache, it can be reused only within the product's allowed 60-second window; without that available copy, use the error response. Reusing a permitted old result avoids database reads and rejecting excess requests keeps them from becoming database work.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.
A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Each unique result is read exactly once, so filling a copy after that read has no future request that can reuse it. The database already meets the stated latency and load needs. The proposal preserves every database read while adding cache writes, memory use, and another copy to manage; checking the cache would also add a lookup with no useful hit. Reconsider if many requests begin repeatedly reading the same inspection results, especially if their database reads become a meaningful latency or load cost. Compare actual response time, database load, hit fraction and miss behavior to determine whether the new reuse pays for the cache.
